papers.title: Bridging Climate Change and Public Health: An Inclusive IVR Framework for Disease Surveillance
papers.venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences and Applications (ACDSA 2026), Boracay Island, Philippines
papers.authors: Segera, Lennox Kahati, Bradley Odimas, Ben Tito
papers.abstract: There is an increase in climate change illnesses such as malaria, cholera, and heat-stress in Kenya and Nigeria, yet so many districts encounter problems in data collection such as: relying on paper logs which reach the public-health offices weeks later, time consuming and costly physical visits. We co-designed an Interactive Voice Response (IVR) system (based on English) that works on any smart-feature phone. Using a mixed-method approach informed by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), we conducted surveys and interviews in Ilaje-Bariga, Lagos. A six-week pilot in North-Central Nigeria (January to April 2025) generated 5660 IVR responses, plus 123 in-person interviews with health workers, patients, and caregivers. Participants were recruited through a purpose-convenience sampling and had to be residents of Ilaje-Bariga aged 18 years and above with healthcare or caregiving experience; those who did not provide consent were excluded. Most (95.1%) had at least secondary education, providing a diverse but locally representative sample of those who can use the english-based version of the IVR. The pilot collected 5,660 clean records. The Task Completion Rate (TCR) was 80.2% and the Not Completing Rate (NCR) 19.8%, with only 691 records needing retries, indicating low errors and latency. A lightweight (native that does not need cloud processing through API (Application Programming Interface) IVR can cut disease-reporting delays from weeks to hours. Next steps include DHIS2 integration and cost-effectiveness testing across Nigerian states.
